acsaRequirement: D060 014M brings RESA expressly within scope — cl. 4.1 requires that defects identified on airside pavements, ASSOCIATED STRIPS OR RESA are assessed for severity and possible effects on operations by a Civil Maintenance Competent Person, documented and investigated — but the procedure states no RESA dimensions, no length, width or grading requirement and no provision standard.
acsaEvidence: Documented and investigated defect records for RESA (D060 014M cl. 4.1)
Three-times-weekly manoeuvring area inspection records covering associated strips
acsaConflict: ACSA's document set contains NO RESA provision, dimension or grading standard at all — RESA is only referenced as an area where defects must be assessed. The check cannot be closed against ACSA's own procedures and must be tested against ICAO Annex 14 / CAR Part 139 directly.
basisNote: Sub-clause numbers within §3.5 were not confirmed this pass; take the 90 m / 240 m length figures from SA-CATS 139 and the Annex 14 amendment current at the audit date.

requirement: Surface Defects e.g Cracks , Rutting , Depression, Shoving e.t.c
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §10.2 — maintenance of pavements: surface kept free of loose material and of irregularities that would impair friction or otherwise affect operations 2. ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual Part 9 (Airport Maintenance Practices) — pavement distress identification, assessment and repair 3. SACAA Civil Aviation Regulations 2011, Part 139 reg 139.02.23 — general duties: runway surfaces maintained under a preventive maintenance programme 4. ASTM D5340 — Standard Test Method for Airport Pavement Condition Index Surveys; the distress catalogue and severity grading ACSA's own PCI surveys run to (industry standard, not statutory)
evidenceExpected:
- Most recent detailed pavement condition/structural survey report (PCI or equivalent) showing crack, rut, depression and shoving severity by pavement section
- Evidence of the routine visual inspection cycle (ideally not exceeding 3 years) feeding into it
target: (TGM §8.9.3) SACAA's own TGM publishes no numeric crack-width/rut-depth pass-fail threshold. It requires (a) routine visual inspection (at least every 3 years recommended, plus the daily/weekly/annual regime) and (b) a detailed structural pavement investigation whenever cracking and/or rutting becomes visually conspicuous. Industry good practice (not SACAA-mandated) grades defects using the FAA/ASTM PCI distress catalog — confirm ACSA's own pavement management methodology matches or documents an equivalent standard.
walkabout: Walk the runway looking for visible cracking, rutting, depression or shoving; note any that appear visually significant and check whether it has a corresponding structural-investigation record. Pass = no conspicuous undocumented distress found and survey within the recommended cycle; fail = conspicuous distress present with no triggered investigation, or survey overdue/incomplete.

requirement: Oppotunistic Defects - Ponding , loose aggregates, vegetation growth in cracks e.t.c
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §2.9 — condition of the movement area and related facilities: assessment and reporting of surface condition, including water on the runway 2. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §10.2 — pavement surface kept free of loose material (stone, aggregate and other debris) 3. ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual Part 2 (Pavement Surface Conditions) — water depth bands, drainage assessment and surface contaminant reporting 4. SACAA Civil Aviation Regulations 2011, Part 139 reg 139.02.23 — general duties: runway surface maintenance and removal of foreign object debris
evidenceExpected:
1. Photographic or written evidence from recent inspections of ponding locations after rainfall

2. Vegetation control / crack-sealing maintenance log showing frequency of clearing loose aggregate and vegetation from joints and cracks
target:
1. (TGM §8.10.2(c)/Table 3) 'Standing water' = more than 25% of the relevant surface area (isolated patches or otherwise) covered by water deeper than 3 mm.

2. (TGM §6.2/§6.3, general) Loose aggregate and vegetation growing in cracks/joints are FOD/surface-defect hazards to be removed under the general obligation to avoid hazardous variations. No numeric threshold exists — qualitative pass/fail.
walkabout:
1. Inspect the surface after rainfall (or review recent post-rainfall photos/records) for pooled water; visually estimate depth and area affected against the 25%/3 mm threshold. Pass = no area meets the standing-water definition; fail = ponding meeting or exceeding the threshold, especially if recurring at the same low spots (possible drainage/grading defect).

2. Inspect cracks/joints and surface for loose aggregate (ravelling) and vegetation growth; check the maintenance log for clearing frequency. Pass = no loose aggregate/vegetation present, or all within a documented recent clearing cycle; fail = vegetation/aggregate visibly present with no recent clearing record.

requirement: Edge of Runway flush with surrounding areas
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §3.4 — runway strips, including the requirement that the strip surface abutting the runway, shoulder or stopway be flush with it 2. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §3.2 — runway shoulders 3. ICAO Doc 9157 Aerodrome Design Manual Part 1 (Runways) — shoulder and strip grading, and the pavement/shoulder interface 4. SACAA Civil Aviation Regulations 2011, Part 139 reg 139.02.10A — physical characteristics as prescribed in Document SA-CATS 139
evidenceExpected:
- Most recent safety area/shoulder inspection record noting the runway edge condition
- Measured survey of the pavement-to-shoulder level difference at representative points along the runway, if available
target: (TGM §6.5.1) The runway edge must adjoin the surrounding safety area/shoulder flush — no step, lip or abrupt level change that could catch a wheel, damage an engine/propeller, or divert drainage. No numeric maximum step height is stated in the TGM; an international ~25 mm benchmark is sometimes used but is NOT a confirmed SACAA figure — do not treat it as a hard limit.
walkabout: Walk the runway edge at representative points, visually and (if available) with a straightedge/measuring tool, checking for a step or lip at the pavement/shoulder interface. Pass = no discernible step/lip; fail = a measurable step, especially if not tracked against any documented tolerance (note: no SACAA numeric tolerance exists, so use the aerodrome's own adopted standard if one exists).

requirement: Asphalt Edge breaks
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §10.2 — maintenance of pavements: surface free of loose material and of hazardous irregularities 2. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §3.2 — runway shoulders, which provide the edge support whose loss produces edge breaks 3. ICAO Doc 9137 Airport Services Manual Part 9 (Airport Maintenance Practices) — pavement edge deterioration and repair 4. COLTO Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Works, Section 4000 (asphalt pavements and seals) — the repair workmanship standard D060 014M itself adopts; industry specification, not statutory
evidenceExpected:
- Recent pavement condition survey noting edge-break locations and severity
- Shoulder construction/maintenance standard ACSA applies (to assess whether edge support is adequate by design)
target: (TGM §6.2.1, general) Asphalt edge breaks fall under the general paved-surface maintenance requirement to prevent harmful irregularities/hazards. No SACAA-published numeric edge-break depth/extent threshold exists; assessed against FOD-generation risk, structural edge support loss, and drainage disruption, commonly benchmarked using the FAA/ASTM PCI 'shoulder/edge' distress category as industry practice.
walkabout: Walk the pavement edge looking for crumbling/broken asphalt, particularly where the shoulder has eroded or settled; check for loose fragments that could become FOD. Pass = no significant edge deterioration, or defects tracked with a documented severity trend; fail = visible edge breaks with no severity tracking or shoulder-support assessment on file.

basisNote: No aviation instrument sets a numeric edge-break depth or extent limit, so the finding must be framed on FOD generation, loss of edge support and drainage disruption rather than on a threshold.

requirement: Runway slopes
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §3.1 — runways: longitudinal slope, slope changes and transverse slope limits, expressed by code number 2. ICAO Doc 9157 Aerodrome Design Manual Part 1 (Runways) — slope design, slope-change transitions and surface drainage 3. SACAA Civil Aviation Regulations 2011, Part 139 reg 139.02.10A — physical characteristics as prescribed in Document SA-CATS 139
evidenceExpected:
- Runway's approved design/as-built longitudinal and transverse profile (survey data or design drawing) showing actual measured slopes
- Cross-check against the aerodrome reference code applicable to that runway
target: Longitudinal slope should not exceed 1% for code 3/4 runways and 2% for code 1/2 runways (with tighter transitional limits near runway ends); transverse slope should be around 1.5% (ideal), not exceeding roughly 1.5–2% for code C–F, up to 2% for code A/B — sufficient for drainage without causing handling difficulty. Figures sourced from a national transposition of Annex 14, not the primary ICAO text — check against the current Annex 14 amendment and the specific runway's code before treating as a hard pass/fail limit.
walkabout: Request/compare the runway's as-built or design survey profile against the applicable code-based slope limits; visually check for localised flat spots or reverse grades at pavement joints/patches that could disrupt drainage even where the overall slope is compliant. Pass = current survey confirms slopes within limits; fail = no current as-built survey available, or reference code changed without re-checking slope compliance.

acsaDocs.title: Friction Testing Procedure (D060 010M)

acsaRequirement: No ACSA procedure states runway longitudinal or transverse slope criteria. The only related requirement is D060 010 cl. 4.6.7: where friction characteristics may be reduced because of poor drainage (INADEQUATE SLOPES OR DEPRESSIONS), an ADDITIONAL friction test shall be done under natural conditions representative of local rain, or the condition may be simulated where testing in natural rain is not possible. D060 014M's monthly inspection covers uneven areas, local depressions and standing water as the observable proxies.
acsaEvidence: Additional wet/natural-rain friction test results under D060 010 cl. 4.6.7
Monthly runway inspection records recording uneven areas, local depressions and standing water
As-built drawings and PMS visual assessment reports

requirement: Check adequacy of Dimensions  & Grading of Safety Areas for each runway

ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §3.4 — runway strips: length before the threshold and beyond the runway end, overall width, and the extent and grading of the graded portion, by code number and approach type 2. requirement: Strength of Strip Areas
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §3.4 — runway strips: the graded portion to be prepared so as to minimise hazards arising from differences in load-bearing capacity to aeroplanes running off the runway, and to support ground vehicles 2. ICAO Doc 9157 Aerodrome Design Manual Part 1 (Runways) — strip preparation, compaction and bearing-strength design 3. SACAA Civil Aviation Regulations 2011, Part 139 reg 139.02.10A — aerodrome physical characteristics as prescribed in Document SA-CATS 139
evidenceExpected:
- Geotechnical design report or CBR (California Bearing Ratio) test results for the runway strip's graded portion
- Any record of rescue and fire fighting (RFF) (rescue and firefighting) vehicle trafficability trials or assessments on the strip
target: The graded portion of the runway strip must be prepared/constructed to minimise hazards from differences in load-bearing capacity between it and the runway pavement (in the event of a runway excursion), and must support rescue/firefighting vehicles and, where relevant, occasional passage of the design aircraft. No single universal CBR value/pass-fail figure was confirmed from primary text — compliance is normally demonstrated through the aerodrome's approved geotechnical design rather than a generic number.
walkabout: This is largely a document-based check, but during the walkabout visually assess the strip's ground condition (softness, saturation, rutting from vehicle use), especially in wet conditions, since a dry-season inspection can miss seasonal weakness. Pass = ground visually firm/trafficable and supported by geotechnical documentation; fail = visibly soft/saturated ground with no supporting test data, or no geotechnical report available at all.
acsaConflict: No ACSA document in the reviewed set addresses the bearing strength or load-carrying capability of runway strips or graded safety areas. D060 014M covers strips only for defect inspection and vegetation; there is no requirement that a strip support an aircraft excursion or a rescue and fire fighting vehicle. This absence is itself the audit finding.
basisNote: No instrument publishes a CBR or other numeric bearing figure for the strip; compliance is demonstrated through the aerodrome's approved geotechnical and pavement design, so the audit test is whether that design documentation exists and is current.

requirement: Check Frangibility objects in Safety areas and Presence of Illegal Objects
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §9.9 — siting of equipment and installations on operational areas: equipment required for air navigation to be mounted as low as practicable and to be frangible 2. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I §3.4 — runway strips: an object not required for air navigation or aircraft safety purposes may not be located on the strip 3. ICAO Doc 9157 Aerodrome Design Manual Part 6 (Frangibility) — frangible mount design, test and certification criteria 4. SACAA Civil Aviation Regulations 2011, Part 139 regs 139.02.10A (obstacle limitation surfaces per SA-CATS 139) and 139.02.32 (protection of navigational aids)
evidenceExpected:
1. Inventory/register of all objects sited within the runway strip and RESA (light fittings, wind cones, signage, poles) noting their frangible-mount certification or design compliance

2. Most recent safety-area walk-down/inspection record checking for unauthorised objects
target:
1. Any object on a runway strip that is required there for air navigation purposes (e.g. approach lights, wind indicators) must be sited/mounted as low as practicable and be frangible (designed to break, distort or yield on impact). Detailed frangible-mount design criteria sit in Doc 9157 Part 6, not verified this pass.

2. No object that is not required for air navigation or aircraft safety purposes may be located on the runway strip at all — such an object is an 'illegal object' regardless of frangibility.
walkabout:
1. Walk the strip/RESA identifying every object present (lights, wind cones, signage, poles); check each against an object register for frangible-mount certification, and visually assess mounting height/rigidity. Pass = every object accounted for in a register with frangibility confirmed; fail = an object present without a frangibility assessment, or no register exists to check against.

2. Walk the strip/RESA looking for anything not on the object register and not clearly serving a navigation/safety function — parked maintenance vehicles, stored materials, temporary construction equipment, informal access tracks. Pass = no unauthorised object present; fail = any unauthorised object found during the walk-down.

Below maintenance-planning level = corrective maintenance must be scheduled; below minimum level = non-compliant, immediate corrective action (typically with a runway condition report/Notice to Airmen (NOTAM)) required.
walkabout: Primarily a document-based check against survey data; during the walkabout, visually note rubber-contaminated or visibly polished/glazed sections of the touchdown zone that commonly correlate with reduced friction, and confirm these are included in the friction survey coverage. Pass = latest survey results meet minimum thresholds, or below-threshold sections have documented corrective action; fail = below-minimum results with no corrective maintenance record, or survey coverage misses high-risk sections.

basis: 1. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(2)(v) and (2)(x) — corrective action where runway friction falls below the minimum friction level 2. question: Walk through what happens when a friction result falls below the maintenance-planning or minimum level — who decides on corrective action, how quickly is it scheduled, and is a NOTAM/runway condition report issued for below-minimum results?

requirement: The surface is maintained in such a condition such as to prevent formation of harmful irregularities
evidenceExpected:
- Latest pavement condition survey report (Pavement Condition Index (PCI)/visual condition survey) for the taxiway
- Weekly/annual inspection records (TGM §8.5–§8.7) noting any surface irregularity findings and remedial work orders raised
target: (CATS 139.02.22(2)(P); TGM §6.2.1, applied to taxiways) The taxiway surface must be kept free of ruts, depressions, humps or other variations that could hazard aircraft, degrade friction/drainage, or cause handling/structural problems. 'Harmful irregularity' is a functional (hazard-based) test, not a fixed numeric limit — severity is graded via engineering assessment.
walkabout: Walk/drive the taxiway, especially heavily-trafficked turning/junction areas, looking, and where available using a straightedge, for ruts/depressions/humps; cross-check against the latest pavement condition survey and inspection records for any noted-but-unremediated irregularities. Pass = no hazardous irregularity found, or all findings have linked work orders showing remediation; fail = visually hazardous irregularity present with no corrective action on file.

Two live procedures give different survey intervals for the same runway.

requirement: Pavement Bearing Strength, Taxiway strength to be equal to that of Runways
basis: 1. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.10(9) — 'a bearing strength of a pavement shall be reported using an aircraft classification rating - pavement classification rating method, as prescribed in Document SA-CATS 139' 2. SA-CATS 139 (technical standard to Part 139) — the prescribed detail of ACR-PCR reporting and of taxiway physical characteristics 3. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 2 (Aerodrome data) — strength of pavements, ACR-PCR reporting for pavements intended for aircraft of apron (ramp) mass above 5 700 kg 4. ICAO Doc 9157 Part 3 (Aerodrome Design Manual — Pavements) — pavement strength evaluation and the ACR-PCR methodology
evidenceExpected:
- Published PCR report/certificate specifically for the taxiway(s) in question
- Traffic mix (aircraft types/ACR) actually using each taxiway, to confirm no ACR exceeds the taxiway's PCR
target: Each pavement is independently classified with its own Pavement Classification Rating (PCR) (row 155). The checklist's stated target of 'taxiway strength equal to that of runways' is a simplification — the correct test is that the taxiway's published PCR must be ≥ the Aircraft Classification Rating (ACR) of every aircraft type regularly using it, not literal numerical equality with the runway's PCR (taxiway loading dynamics differ from runway loading).
walkabout: Primarily a document-based check against the taxiway-specific PCR report; during the walkabout, note any signs of unusually concentrated or heavy loading (e.g. push-back/turning areas) that should be reflected in the bearing-strength evaluation.

acsaRequirement: No ACSA procedure states a taxiway bearing strength requirement or a rule that taxiway strength must equal runway strength. D060 014M treats Taxiway (TWY) and Taxilane (TLN) in the same frequency matrix as the runway — monthly inspection, three-yearly visual assessment and condition-driven structural integrity evaluation of the pavement and its sub-layers — with structural investigation triggered when relatively large cracks and/or rutting appear, or after rehabilitation, or when traffic changes.
acsaEvidence: Structural integrity evaluation (PMS) reports for the taxiway pavement and its sub-layers
PCI Survey (ASTM D5340) report (5 years)
Three-yearly detailed visual assessment (PMS) reports
acsaConflict: ACSA publishes no bearing strength values or PCN for any pavement, and no requirement that taxiway strength match the runway; and Version 6 removed the fixed structural evaluation cycle, leaving no calendar interval at which taxiway strength is re-established.
basisNote: ACR-PCR replaced ACN-PCN with effect from 28 November 2024, and each pavement is rated in its own right — the test is taxiway PCR ≥ ACR of the aircraft using it, not numerical equality with the runway.

requirement: Surface Defects e.g Cracks , Rutting , Depression, Shoving e.t.c
basis: 1. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(2)(a)(i) — a maintenance programme, including preventive maintenance, to keep facilities in a condition that does not impair the safety, regularity or efficiency of air navigation 2. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(8)(d)(ii) — reporting of rough or broken surfaces on a runway, taxiway or apron 3. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 10, §10.2 Pavements — movement area surfaces inspected and monitored regularly, surfaces kept free of harmful irregularities 4. TMH 9 (COTO, 2016) Manual for Visual Assessment of Road Pavements, Parts A and B — distress nomenclature and severity grading (recommended practice, not statutory)
evidenceExpected:
- Most recent detailed pavement condition/structural survey report (PCI or equivalent) showing crack, rut, depression and shoving severity by pavement section
- Evidence of the routine visual inspection cycle (ideally not exceeding 3 years) feeding into it
target: (TGM §8.9.3) SACAA's own TGM publishes no numeric crack-width/rut-depth pass-fail threshold. It requires (a) routine visual inspection (at least every 3 years recommended, plus the daily/weekly/annual regime) and (b) a detailed structural pavement investigation whenever cracking and/or rutting becomes visually conspicuous. Industry good practice (not SACAA-mandated) grades defects using the FAA/ASTM PCI distress catalog — confirm ACSA's own pavement management methodology matches or documents an equivalent standard.
walkabout: Walk the runway looking for visible cracking, rutting, depression or shoving; note any that appear visually significant and check whether it has a corresponding structural-investigation record. Pass = no conspicuous undocumented distress found and survey within the recommended cycle; fail = conspicuous distress present with no triggered investigation, or survey overdue/incomplete.

basisNote: Neither Annex 14 nor Part 139 publishes a numeric crack-width or rut-depth limit; the grading standard is whatever ACSA's pavement management methodology documents, commonly TMH 9 locally or ASTM D5340 for airport pavements.

requirement: Oppotunistic Defects - Ponding , loose aggregates, vegetation growth in cracks e.t.c
basis: 1. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(2)(y) and (2)(z) — standing water, mud, dust, sand, rubber deposits and other contaminants to be completely removed, and taxiways kept clear of contaminants 2. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(8)(d)(iv) — reporting of water on a runway, taxiway or apron 3. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 10, §10.2 Pavements — regular inspection with the objective of avoiding and eliminating loose objects or debris that might damage aircraft or impair aircraft systems 4. ICAO Doc 9137 Part 9 (Airport Services Manual — Airport Maintenance Practices) — pavement drainage, crack sealing and control of vegetation in pavement joints
evidenceExpected:
1. Photographic or written evidence from recent inspections of ponding locations after rainfall

2. Vegetation control / crack-sealing maintenance log showing frequency of clearing loose aggregate and vegetation from joints and cracks
target:
1. (TGM §8.10.2(c)/Table 3) 'Standing water' = more than 25% of the relevant surface area (isolated patches or otherwise) covered by water deeper than 3 mm.

2. (TGM §6.2/§6.3, general) Loose aggregate and vegetation growing in cracks/joints are FOD/surface-defect hazards to be removed under the general obligation to avoid hazardous variations. No numeric threshold exists — qualitative pass/fail.
walkabout:
1. Inspect the surface after rainfall (or review recent post-rainfall photos/records) for pooled water; visually estimate depth and area affected against the 25%/3 mm threshold. Pass = no area meets the standing-water definition; fail = ponding meeting or exceeding the threshold, especially if recurring at the same low spots (possible drainage/grading defect).

2. Inspect cracks/joints and surface for loose aggregate (ravelling) and vegetation growth; check the maintenance log for clearing frequency. Pass = no loose aggregate/vegetation present, or all within a documented recent clearing cycle; fail = vegetation/aggregate visibly present with no recent clearing record.

requirement: Edge of Taxiway flush with surrounding areas
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 3 — Taxiway strips: the surface of the strip should be flush at the edge of the taxiway or shoulder, with no hazardous step 2. Pass = no discernible step; fail = a measurable step, especially where narrower/less robust taxiway shoulders show settlement.

requirement: Asphalt Edge breaks
basis: 1. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(2)(a)(i) and (8)(d)(ii) — preventive maintenance programme and reporting of rough or broken surfaces on a runway, taxiway or apron 2. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 10, §10.2 Pavements — surfaces inspected regularly to avoid and eliminate loose objects or debris, and kept free of harmful irregularities 3. ICAO Doc 9137 Part 9 (Airport Maintenance Practices) — asphalt pavement distress identification and repair practice 4. COLTO Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Works (1998), 4000 series (asphalt pavements and seals) — repair materials and workmanship (recommended practice, not statutory)
evidenceExpected:
- Recent pavement condition survey noting edge-break locations and severity
- Shoulder construction/maintenance standard ACSA applies (to assess whether edge support is adequate by design)
target: (TGM §6.2.1, general) Asphalt edge breaks fall under the general paved-surface maintenance requirement to prevent harmful irregularities/hazards. No SACAA-published numeric edge-break depth/extent threshold exists; assessed against FOD-generation risk, structural edge support loss, and drainage disruption, commonly benchmarked using the FAA/ASTM PCI 'shoulder/edge' distress category as industry practice.

Pass = no significant edge deterioration, or defects tracked with a documented severity trend; fail = visible edge breaks with no severity tracking or shoulder-support assessment on file.

requirement: Taxiway slopes allow for drainage
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 3 — Taxiway slopes: longitudinal slope not exceeding 1.5 per cent where the code letter is C, D, E or F and 3 per cent where it is A or B, with transverse slopes sufficient to prevent accumulation of water 2. ICAO Doc 9157 Part 2 (Taxiways, Aprons and Holding Bays) — taxiway geometric design and surface drainage 3. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(2)(w) — action where the drainage characteristics of the surface are such that friction may be impaired under precipitation 4. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(2)(y) — complete removal of standing water from the movement area
evidenceExpected:
- Taxiway's design cross-section/longitudinal profile showing intended drainage slope
- Post-rainfall inspection records or photos confirming no ponding occurs on the taxiway surface
target: (ICAO Annex 14 §3.7 taxiway slope Standard; TGM §6.8.1) Taxiway transverse/longitudinal slopes must be adequate to shed surface water to the drainage system without ponding, generally aligned with runway-order-of-magnitude transverse slopes (≈1–1.5%, code-dependent). The general drainage-function requirement (drains not blocked, system performs as designed) is confirmed; the specific taxiway slope percentage from Annex 14 is not independently re-verified.
walkabout: Inspect the taxiway after rainfall (or review post-rainfall records/photos) for ponding; where a design cross-section is available, compare against it. Pass = no ponding and slope consistent with design; fail = ponding present despite a compliant design slope (suggesting a downstream blockage) or no design cross-section available to check against.

D060 010 cl. 4.6.7 requires an additional friction test under natural rain conditions where friction may be reduced by inadequate slopes or depressions.

Monthly taxiway inspection records recording standing water and stormwater blockages
Additional wet-condition friction test results (D060 010 cl. 4.6.7)

requirement: Check adequacy of Dimensions  & Grading of Safety Areas for the Code of the Associated Taxiway
basis: 1. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 3 — Taxiway strips: the strip extends symmetrically each side of the taxiway centre line to the distance given in Table 3-1 for the code letter, with a graded central portion 2. ICAO Doc 9157 Part 2 (Taxiways, Aprons and Holding Bays) — taxiway strip width, grading and object clearance guidance 3. SACAA CAR Part 139 and SA-CATS 139 — physical characteristics of taxiways and taxiway strips prescribed in the technical standard for the aerodrome licence category
evidenceExpected:
- Taxiway design layout drawing showing graded strip width for its aerodrome reference code letter
- Recent survey confirming actual graded extent and freedom from obstructing objects
target: Graded taxiway strip/safety area must extend from the taxiway centre line by a distance set by code letter: approx. A ≈ 15.5 m, B ≈ 20 m, C ≈ 26 m, D ≈ 37 m, E ≈ 43.5 m, F ≈ 51 m (double for total strip width). Confirm against the current Annex 14 amendment and the specific taxiway's code letter before applying as a hard limit.
walkabout: Walk the graded strip either side of the taxiway; compare against the design drawing for the taxiway's code letter, checking for encroachment by fencing, lighting infrastructure or vegetation. Pass = graded extent matches design and is unobstructed; fail = encroachment present, code letter reclassified upward without widening, or no current survey available.

requirement: Oppotunistic Defects - Ponding , loose aggregates, vegetation growth in cracks e.t.c
basis: 1. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(2)(y) and (2)(aa) — complete removal of standing water, dust, sand, oil, rubber deposits and other contaminants, and aprons kept clear of contaminants 2. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 10, §10.2 Pavements — inspection and condition monitoring with the objective of avoiding and eliminating loose objects or debris that might damage aircraft 3. evidenceExpected:
1. Photographic or written evidence from recent inspections of ponding locations after rainfall

2. Vegetation control / crack-sealing maintenance log showing frequency of clearing loose aggregate and vegetation from joints and cracks
target:
1. (TGM §8.10.2(c)/Table 3) 'Standing water' = more than 25% of the relevant surface area (isolated patches or otherwise) covered by water deeper than 3 mm.

walkabout:
1. Inspect the surface after rainfall (or review recent post-rainfall photos/records) for pooled water; visually estimate depth and area affected against the 25%/3 mm threshold. Pass = no area meets the standing-water definition; fail = ponding meeting or exceeding the threshold, especially if recurring at the same low spots (possible drainage/grading defect).

2. Inspect cracks/joints and surface for loose aggregate (ravelling) and vegetation growth; check the maintenance log for clearing frequency. Pass = no loose aggregate/vegetation present, or all within a documented recent clearing cycle; fail = vegetation/aggregate visibly present with no recent clearing record.

requirement: Corner breaks & Joint sealant failure
basis: 1. SACAA CAR Part 139, reg 139.02.23(2)(a)(i) — maintenance programme, including preventive maintenance, for facilities including concrete apron pavements 2. ICAO Annex 14 Vol I, Ch 10, §10.2 Pavements — surfaces kept free of harmful irregularities and of loose debris, which spalled corners and extruded sealant generate 3. ICAO Doc 9157 Part 3 (Aerodrome Design Manual — Pavements) — rigid pavement jointing, joint sealing and resealing 4. ASTM D5340, Standard Test Method for Airport Pavement Condition Index Surveys — defines 'corner break' and 'joint seal damage' and their low/medium/high severity grading (industry practice, not statutory)
evidenceExpected:
1. ACSA's pavement management system methodology/distress manual reference (confirming whether it follows FAA PAVER/ASTM D5340 or an equivalent), and the apron condition survey's specific findings on corner breaks by slab/panel

2. Apron condition survey's specific findings on joint sealant condition by slab/panel
target:
1. A 'corner break' is a crack intersecting the joints near a rigid-pavement slab corner, isolating a triangular piece — a standard rigid (concrete) pavement distress type, severity-graded (low/medium/high) in the FAA/ASTM Pavement Condition Index (PCI) catalog. No SACAA numeric threshold exists — confirm ACSA's own pavement management/consulting engineer's standard as the actual applied criterion.

2. 'Joint sealant failure' is loss of adhesion/cohesion or extrusion of joint sealant, allowing water/incompressible material intrusion. No SACAA numeric threshold — confirm ACSA's applied standard.
question: 2. Is joint-sealant resealing tracked as a scheduled preventive-maintenance item, or only done reactively once failure is visible?
walkabout:
1. Walk concrete slab pavement (apron) checking slab corners for cracks intersecting joints and isolating a triangular piece; note severity (extent of displacement/looseness). Pass = no corner breaks, or all identified and severity-classified in the survey; fail = corner breaks present without severity classification or a referenced distress standard.

2. Inspect slab joints for cracked, missing or extruded sealant; check whether resealing is logged as a scheduled maintenance item rather than ad-hoc housekeeping. Pass = sealant intact or a documented resealing programme is in place; fail = visibly failed sealant with no resealing programme, risking accelerated corner-break damage.

acsaRequirement: ACSA requires no bearing strength report as such. D060 014M cl. 4.1 requires that a pavement structural investigation be conducted WHEN RELATIVELY LARGE CRACKS AND/OR RUTTING IN THE SURFACING APPEARS, and that EVALUATION IS REQUIRED AFTER PAVEMENT REHABILITATION OR WHEN TRAFFIC CHANGES AS COMPARED TO THE INITIAL TRAFFIC — the closest ACSA equivalent to a post-construction strength report, with the SACAA TGM: For the Calculation of Pavement Bearing Strength cited as the authority. D060 010 cl. 4.6.10 does impose a hard post-construction control on the surface: friction testing after any rehabilitation, resurfacing, surface treatment or new pavement construction, undertaken PRIOR TO the pavement being returned to operational service, with corrective action VERIFIED BY REPEAT FRICTION TESTING before release.

acsaConflict: No ACSA document in the reviewed set of 99 mentions PCN, ACN, pavement classification, publication of bearing strength in the AIP, or the control of overload operations. The only trace is the SACAA TGM: For the Calculation of Pavement Bearing Strength listed as a referenced standard in D060 014M. ACSA has no internal procedure governing PCN publication currency or overload approvals — a material governance gap given CAR Part 139 and ICAO Annex 14 Chapter 2 obligations.

requirement: Remove contaminants as rapidly as posible and completely as posible
basis: SA_CATS 139 (2) U(139.02.22) & TGM for Civil Infrastructure
evidenceExpected:
1. Rubber/contaminant removal work order log for the last 12 months (dates, method used, area treated, and time elapsed from detection to completion)

2. Any incident/spill report for fuel or oil contamination showing response time, and confirmation that cleanup sand was removed after use
target:
1. Rubber must be removed as rapidly and completely as practicable. Confirmed methods/parameters: high-pressure water blasting at 350–700 kg/cm², productivity ≈278 m² per hour per unit (a typical 900 m × 24 m touchdown zone ≈100 hours per unit); hot compressed air exhausting at ~400 m/s at ~1,200°C; chemical solvents applied, left up to one hour, then washed/swept off.

2. Fuel/oil spillage, and any sand used to clean it up, must be removed as rapidly and completely as practicable — sand left in place is itself a turbine engine/propeller ingestion hazard.
walkabout:
1. requirement: Daily , Weekly, Annual and Special  inspections
basis: TGM 6 and SA-CATS 139
evidenceExpected:
1. Daily inspection log (should show a minimum of 3 entries/day)

2. Weekly detailed pavement inspection record

3. Most recent annual inspection report signed off by a qualified civil engineer

4. Special inspection reports (post-complaint, post-construction, post-grass-cutting), including inspection team composition records
target:
1. A minimum of 3 inspections per day must be conducted of the movement area; inspection from a moving vehicle at a suitable speed is permitted.

2. All aerodrome pavements within the movement area must be inspected in more detail at least once a week, with particular focus on high-load areas (departure taxiways, apron parking stands, take-off taxiways, runway intersections, runway touchdown areas).

3. All pavements within the movement area must be inspected at least once a year by a professionally qualified (civil) engineer.

4. Special inspections must be conducted after receipt of a complaint or an unusual condition/event, after construction activity, after grass cutting (specifically to confirm all cut grass is removed), and for unique aircraft operations. Inspection teams overall must include at least one person qualified in civil engineering/the built environment.
walkabout:
1. Review the daily inspection log for the audit period and count entries per day; if practical, observe or shadow one inspection round in progress. Pass = ≥3 logged inspections every day with no unexplained gaps; fail = days with fewer than 3 inspections and no documented reason or catch-up inspection.

2. Request the weekly inspection record and, during the walkabout, check the named high-load areas (departure taxiways, stands, take-off taxiways, intersections, touchdown zones) for evidence of recent detailed inspection (e.g. chalk marks, freshly noted findings). Pass = weekly record demonstrably covers and emphasises the named high-load areas; fail = weekly record generic, with no clear focus on those areas.

3. Check whether the current annual inspection report's scope still covers all pavements presently in use, with no new/expanded areas omitted.

4. During the walkabout, check for any recently cut grass areas and confirm clippings have been fully removed (a specific §8.8.3 trigger); request the most recent special inspection records tied to any recent complaint, construction activity or unusual event and check team composition. Pass = special inspections documented for all applicable trigger events with qualified personnel; fail = a trigger event (e.g. recent grass cutting) with no corresponding special inspection record, or no evidence of qualified personnel on the team.

The procedure also states no numeric fence voltage limit ('within design range' only) and its IAL/PID frequency table is internally contradictory (rows labelled 'Monthly (W)' / 'Weekly (W)'). No ACSA document in the reviewed set covers perimeter patrol records, clear zones or gate access control — those belong to AVSEC procedures not in this set.

requirement: Certificates in Respect of Building
basis: National Building Standards Act 103 of 1977
evidenceExpected: A single file/register per building listing all certificates held for it: Certificate of Occupancy, electrical CoC, fire installation Form 4/compliance certificate, structural Form 4; the building's current use and floor layout noted alongside the register.
target: National Building Regulations & Building Standards Act 103 of 1977 is the umbrella statute: plans must be approved before construction (ss4 & 7), and no building may lawfully be occupied without a Certificate of Occupancy (s14), which itself depends on the electrical and structural completion certificates (SANS 10400-A forms) having been submitted.
walkabout: Walk the building and compare its current use and floor layout (tenants, subdivisions, extensions) against what the certificate register says it should be; flag any mismatch that would require a fresh certificate.
acsaConflict: NO ACSA procedure requires a Certificate in Respect of Building (National Building Regulations / Building Standards Act s14). D080 028M is ACSA's buildings procedure and its records table (cl. 11) lists only inspection records and asset strategy forms ME 038-041 - no statutory building certificate. The only certificate regime ACSA writes down for buildings is the electrical COC in D060 004M and the yearly validation of 'Council-approved designs of the existing installations' for fire installations in D080 002M cl. 4.7.8. Raise as an ACSA documentation gap, not merely a KSIA evidence gap.

requirement: Occupancy Certificate
basis: 1. National Building Regulations and Building Standards Act 103 of 1977 s14(1) — the local authority must issue a certificate of occupancy once satisfied the building was erected in accordance with the Act and the conditions of the s7 approval 2. NBR&BS Act s14(1)(a), read with s14(2) and, where applicable, s14(2A) — the electrical installation certificate and the approved competent person's certificate (SANS 10400-A Form 4) must be lodged before a certificate of occupancy may be issued 3. NBR&BS Act s14(4)(a) — offence for the owner or an interested person to occupy or use, or permit the occupation or use of, a building for which no certificate of occupancy has been issued 4. National Building Regulations reg A20, read with SANS 10400-A — classification and designation of occupancies; a change of use or added occupancy (retail in circulation space, a new pier) changes the class certified and requires the approval and certificate to be revisited
evidenceExpected: The building's original Certificate of Occupancy (erf number, building description, approved use); proof (a further CoC or plan-approval record) for any subsequent alteration, extension or change of use.
target: A Certificate of Occupancy (NBR&BS Act s14) must be issued by the local municipal building control authority before lawful occupation; occupying without one is a criminal offence. It is a once-off certificate per building/erf, not periodically renewed, but a fresh certificate is required after any alteration or change of use needing new plan approval.
walkabout: Walk the building's floor layout and compare current use/tenanting (e.g. retail units added in circulation areas, a new pier or extension) against the use and layout described on the Certificate of Occupancy.
acsaConflict: No ACSA document in the 99-document set requires an Occupancy Certificate to be held or renewed. The nearest reference is D060 020M cl. 4.7 (Asset Modification), which lists 'submission for occupancy certificate' as step (g) of the ten mandatory steps for tenant-initiated modifications - so ACSA requires an occupancy certificate to be OBTAINED for new tenant works but never requires existing buildings to hold one.
basisNote: Occupation under a written local-authority permission granted pending issue of the certificate is time-limited and conditional and is not a substitute for the certificate itself.

requirement: Certificates of Competence- Electrical
basis: 1. OHS Act 85 of 1993, Electrical Installation Regulations 2009 reg 7(1) — every user or lessor must hold a valid certificate of compliance in the form of Annexure 1 with an approved test report; reg 7(4) — a further CoC for any addition or alteration; reg 7(5) — no change of ownership on a CoC older than two years 2. Electrical Installation Regulations 2009 reg 9, read with reg 11 — only a registered person (electrical tester for single-phase LV, installation electrician, master installation electrician) may issue a CoC, and may not issue one where the installation does not comply 3. SANS 10142-1 — the wiring code incorporated under the Electrical Installation Regulations (reg 5, design and construction); the standard against which the installation is inspected and tested for the CoC 4. OHS Act, General Machinery Regulations reg 2(1) — written full-time designation of a competent person to supervise machinery, with the qualification tier set by reg 2(4) (installed power, kW) and reg 2(5) (electricity distribution capacity, kVA)
evidenceExpected: Current electrical CoC for the building/installation, issued by a registered person; the underlying test report; any supplementary CoC(s) for additions/alterations made since the original.
target: Every electrical installation must be covered by a valid Certificate of Compliance issued by a person registered with the Department of Employment and Labour/Electrical Contracting Board, following inspection and testing to SANS 10142-1 (Electrical Installation Regulations 2009 under the OHS Act). Any addition or alteration requires a new supplementary CoC for the existing CoC to remain valid for the whole installation. No fixed statutory expiry while unchanged, but a CoC older than 2 years is generally treated as needing re-verification on change of ownership/use — confirm ACSA's own internal re-inspection interval for terminal buildings.
walkabout: Inspect the distribution board(s)/installation for any visible addition or alteration (new DB, tenant fit-out wiring) and check it is covered by a supplementary CoC on file; note the registered person's details on the CoC for verification.

requirement: Certificates of Competence- Fire
basis: 1. National Building Regulations regs T1(2) and W4, read with reg A19 — fire protection and the fire installation may be met by rational design, for which the owner must appoint an approved competent person (SANS 10400-A Form 2) who certifies on completion (Form 4) 2. SANS 10400-T (fire protection) and SANS 10400-W (fire installation) — the deemed-to-satisfy requirements the design, hazard classification and installation are certified against 3. SANS 10105-1 (use and control of fire-fighting equipment), SANS 10139 (fire detection and alarm systems), SANS 10287 (automatic sprinkler installations) and SANS 10114-2 (emergency lighting) — the inspection, servicing and testing regimes for the installed components 4. OHS Act, Environmental Regulations for Workplaces reg 9(2) — adequate suitable fire-fighting equipment at strategic locations or as recommended by the local fire chief, maintained in good working order; Fire Brigade Services Act 99 of 1987 and the eThekwini Fire Prevention and Flammable Liquids and Substances By-law — the municipal fire compliance and annual renewal regime
evidenceExpected: 1. Original SANS 10400-A Form 4 fire-system completion certificate. 2. Current (within 12 months) fire compliance certificate; extinguisher service tags; fire detection/alarm annual test certificate; sprinkler annual flow-test certificate; emergency lighting discharge-test certificate.
target: Two distinct certificates. 1. Fire Installation Design/Construction Certificate: SANS 10400-A Form 4, signed once-off at completion by the competent person certifying the fire protection system was built to SANS 10400-T. 2. Annual Fire Compliance & Component Servicing: most municipal fire authorities require annual (12-month) renewal of the building's fire compliance certificate, plus component servicing at set intervals — extinguishers: monthly visual + annual service (SANS 1475-1); detection/alarm: quarterly zone test + annual full test (SANS 10139); sprinklers: weekly visual + annual flow test (SANS 10287); emergency lighting: annual full discharge test (SANS 10114-2). Exact by-law/authority varies per ACSA airport city.
walkabout: 2. Physically check extinguisher service tags for current-year dates, sprinkler/hydrant service tags, and emergency lighting discharge-test labels on a sample of units; check the monthly visual-inspection log book is kept and matches what is found on the units.

requirement: Certificates of Competence- Structural System
basis: 1. National Building Regulations reg A19 — the owner must appoint and retain one or more approved competent persons for rational design or rational assessment, including the inspections and certifications required; SANS 10400-A Form 2 (appointment) and Form 4 (certificate of completion) 2. National Building Regulations Part B, read with SANS 10400-B — structural design requirements the competent person designs and certifies the structural system against 3. OHS Act 85 of 1993, Construction Regulations 2014 reg 11(2) — the owner of a structure must have it inspected periodically by competent persons, at least once every six months for the first two years and yearly thereafter, keep it safe for continued use and retain the inspection and maintenance records 4. Engineering Profession Act 46 of 2000 — ECSA registration as Professional Engineer or Professional Certificated Engineer, the registration on which the 'competent person' definition rests
evidenceExpected: SANS 10400-A Form 4 (Certificate of Completion of the Structural System); evidence of the appointed engineer's ECSA registration at the time of appointment.
target: A structural engineer registered with ECSA as Professional Engineer (or Professional Certificated Engineer) is appointed competent person for the structural system (SANS 10400-A Form 2), and on completion signs Form 4 certifying it was designed and constructed per the approved application. Required at original construction and again whenever structural alteration needs fresh plan approval; existing ACSA buildings normally rely on periodic structural condition assessments (see concrete/alignment checks below) rather than a recurring competence certificate.
walkabout: Where structural alterations are visible on site (added floors, altered load paths, new structural elements), check whether an updated Form 4/engineer's certification exists for that altered portion.

acsaRequirement: D080 028M requires a three-monthly visual structural inspection (foundations for sagging, walls for cracks, water damage and expansion, roofs, gutters and drop boxes), then a six-monthly structural inspection and a yearly structural integrity inspection on all B&FM maintainable assets, which 'as applicable... shall be carried out by a COMPETENT PERSON in line with the Construction Regulations of the OHS Act'. Appointment of the competent person at each tier is triggered by the outcome of the preceding lower-tier inspection.

Competent person appointed 'in line with the Construction Regulations of the OHS Act' - D080 028M cl. 4.2.5 miscites this as 'the OHS Act of 1995'; the Act is No. 85 of 1993.

requirement: Assess Surface Condition of Concrete (Corrosion, Cracking, Delamination, Scaling, Spalling, Popouts, Exposed Reinforcement, etc)
basis: ACI 201.1R-08 (Guide for Conducting a Visual Inspection of Concrete in Service)
evidenceExpected: Most recent structural condition/visual survey report, prepared by a registered engineer or competent inspector, rating each defect type; ACSA's internal procedure setting the required inspection interval.
target: ACI 201.1R-08 (Guide for Conducting a Visual Inspection of Concrete in Service) provides a structured method and severity-rating scale for corrosion staining, cracking, delamination, scaling, spalling, popouts and exposed reinforcement. No mandatory SANS document covers visual condition surveys of in-service concrete, so ACI 201.1R is the de facto standard used by SA structural engineers. No SA law mandates a specific inspection interval — confirm ACSA's own internal condition-assessment frequency (commonly annual or biennial for critical structures).
walkabout: Walk accessible concrete surfaces (columns, soffits, beams, slabs) for corrosion staining, cracking, delamination (sounding/tap-test where feasible), scaling, spalling, popouts and exposed reinforcement, and compare against the findings/ratings in the latest survey.

requirement: Assess Distress Indicators(Cracking, Staining, Leaking, etc)
basis: 1. OHS Act 85 of 1993, Construction Regulations 2014 reg 11(2)(a)–(d) — periodic competent-person inspection of the structure, maintenance in a condition that remains safe for continued use, and retention of the inspection and maintenance records 2. NBR&BS Act 103 of 1977 s12 — local authority's power to require demolition, alteration or securing of a building that is or will probably be dangerous to life or property, and to bar occupation or use pending written permission; s21 — magistrate's order in support 3. OHS Act 85 of 1993 s8(1) and s9(1) — safe working environment, and the duty toward persons other than employees (passengers, tenants and concessionaires in a terminal) affected by the state of the structure 4. ACI PRC-201.1-08 (published as ACI 201.1R-08), Guide for Conducting a Visual Inspection of Concrete in Service — the methodology ACSA works to; US professional guidance and recommended practice, not statutory in South Africa
evidenceExpected: Distress-indicator findings section of the structural inspection report (cracking, staining, leaking); where flagged as potentially unsafe, evidence of notification to the local authority/ACSA engineering and of remedial action taken.
target: No separate SA statutory standard exists for distress indicators (cracking, staining, leaking); assessed under the same ACI 201.1R-08 visual-inspection methodology by a competent/registered structural engineer. A finding suggesting the structure may be unsafe can trigger the local authority's dangerous-building powers under NBR&BS Act ss12/13, requiring remedial works or restricted use pending repair.
walkabout: Look for visible cracking, staining or leaking on structural elements and facades, and check whether any such observation is already logged in the inspection report or has an open remedial job card linked to it.

acsaRequirement: D080 028M requires the three-monthly visual structural inspection to check walls for cracks, signs of water damage and expansion, and all roofs for damage including failed waterproofing systems, and requires a DAILY inspection of areas inside and outside the building where B&FM assets are maintained, with any defect reported to the IMC and D060 016M followed. D060 016M requires every fault to be logged on Oracle eAM with the Date of Call and Time of Call captured and a Work Request Number issued.

Daily corrective-maintenance inspection records
Oracle eAM work requests / work orders with date and time of call
Signed hard-copy work orders scanned into Oracle eAM and filed at the IMC
acsaConflict: No severity classification for distress indicators and no defect response times for buildings. By contrast D060 012M cl. 4.5 does set stormwater defect response times (blocked runway/taxiway inlet within 2 hours, ponding same operational day, structural collapse risk immediate barricade plus 24-hour repair plan) - so ACSA has demonstrated it can set them and has simply not done so for buildings.

requirement: Assess Alignment of Structure (Settlement, Deflection, Expansion, Contraction, etc)
basis: 1. OHS Act 85 of 1993, Construction Regulations 2014 reg 11(2) — owner's duty to have the structure inspected periodically by competent persons (at least six-monthly for the first two years, yearly thereafter), keep it safe for continued use and retain the records 2. SANS 10160-1, Basis of structural design and actions for buildings and industrial structures — serviceability limit states against which settlement, deflection and thermal movement are judged (cited at document level) 3. ISO 13822, Bases for design of structures — Assessment of existing structures — recognised method for assessing an existing structure against its original design basis; international guidance, not statutory in South Africa 4. NBR&BS Act 103 of 1977 s12 — dangerous-building powers where progressive movement indicates the structure may be unsafe
evidenceExpected: Survey or monitoring records (visual or instrumented — crack-width monitors, level surveys) assessing settlement, deflection, expansion/contraction against the structure's design serviceability limits, with engineer's sign-off.
target: No single SA statutory inspection standard exists for structural alignment; movement (settlement, deflection, expansion/contraction) is assessed by a registered structural engineer against the serviceability limits in SANS 10160-1 and the original design code, typically via visual and/or instrumented survey. A structure exceeding serviceability limits or showing progressive settlement can trigger NBR&BS Act dangerous-structure provisions (ss12/13). No SA statute prescribes a survey frequency — ACSA's internal procedure governs.
walkabout: Check any installed movement-monitoring devices (crack-width monitors, level-survey points) are being read/recorded on schedule, and visually inspect known movement joints/cracks for width or progression against the last recorded reading.

acsaRequirement: D080 028M requires the three-monthly visual structural inspection to 'check foundations for signs of sagging' and to check walls for cracks, water damage and expansion, and requires a yearly structural integrity inspection on all B&FM maintainable assets, carried out where applicable by a competent person appointed under the Construction Regulations, triggered by the outcome of the six-monthly structural inspection.
acsaThreshold: Foundation sagging check: Three Monthly (3M). Structural inspection: Six Monthly (6M). Structural integrity inspection: Yearly (Y) (D080 028M cl. 4.2.2 / 4.2.5).

acsaConflict: ACSA states no measurable limits for settlement, deflection, expansion or contraction, no survey or monitoring-point requirement, and no trigger value at which a competent person MUST be appointed - the appointment is left entirely to the 'outcome' of the preceding inspection with no defined threshold, which makes the escalation unenforceable.
basisNote: No South African instrument prescribes a movement-survey frequency or a numeric settlement limit for an existing building, so the audit test is the recorded design basis and the SANS 10160-1 serviceability criteria, not a published threshold.

requirement: Check controls for " Objectionable Discharge"
basis: 1. National Building Regulations reg P3 (control of objectionable discharge) and reg P4 (industrial effluent), read with SANS 10400-P — the drainage installation may not discharge in a manner that is objectionable or a health hazard 2. eThekwini Municipality Sewage Disposal By-law, 2016 s6 (objectionable discharge) and s25 (permission to discharge trade effluent), with the acceptance limits in Schedules A and B — the by-law and permit, not ACSA's procedure, carry the numeric limits 3. Water Services Act 108 of 1997 s7 — industrial effluent may be disposed of only in the manner approved by the water services authority or provider; s21 — the by-laws under which the discharge permit is issued 4. National Water Act 36 of 1998 s21(f) and s21(g) — discharging waste into a water resource, and disposing of waste in a manner that may detrimentally impact a water resource, are licensable water uses; s19 — duty to prevent and remedy pollution, engaged by contaminated stormwater
evidenceExpected: Records showing the drainage installation's trap/vent configuration matches approved design (as-built drawings); any record of nuisance/odour/pollution complaints or incidents and their resolution.
target: SANS 10400-P Regulation P3 prohibits any drainage installation from discharging effluent in a manner that creates a nuisance, health hazard, or pollutes a water source — traps, vents and treatment provisions must prevent odorous, contaminating or offensive discharge. Can also engage the applicable municipal Wastewater/Sewage Disposal By-law and National Water Act effluent-quality provisions where surface water is affected.
walkabout: Inspect accessible traps and vents for correct installation and condition, and note any odour at drainage outlets or discharge points; cross-check against the maintenance log for related complaints.

acsaRequirement: T050 005M cl. 4.3 requires all industrial effluent to be discharged to the effluent drainage system, prohibits discharge to ground or stormwater under any circumstances, and requires the Maintenance and Engineering Manager to ensure effluent is discharged at the final discharge points in accordance with the effluent discharge permit requirements and 'especially the effluent quality standards stipulated in the effluent discharge permit'. Cl. 4.4 prohibits any effluent discharge to a stormwater facility and requires contaminated stormwater to be diverted into the effluent system with measures to prevent recurrence.
acsaThreshold: The numeric limits are NOT in the procedure: 'in accordance with the effluent discharge permit requirements and especially the effluent quality standards stipulated in the effluent discharge permit' (T050 005M cl. 4.3). The permit, not ACSA's procedure, carries the objectionable-discharge limits. Stormwater quality monitoring 'where possible on a bi-annual basis during the rainy seasons or as long as stormwater is flowing', tested by accredited laboratories using SABS methods (T050 005M cl. 4.4).
acsaEvidence: KSIA effluent discharge permit with its stated effluent quality standards
Register of Effluent and Storm Water Discharge Points - EMS 105
Effluent quality analysis monitoring schedule and analysis results
Accredited-laboratory stormwater analyses (SABS methods)
acsaConflict: T050 005M requires an 'effluent quality analysis monitoring schedule' to be implemented but states NO sampling interval for effluent - only stormwater carries the bi-annual rainy-season figure. The permit must therefore be obtained to establish both the limits and the frequency.
basisNote: T050 005M cl. 4.3 defers the quality limits to 'the effluent discharge permit'; the permit takes its limits from the eThekwini Sewage Disposal By-law schedules, so the by-law is the auditable standard behind the permit.

requirement: Check Records for Odour Control
basis: 1. National Building Regulations reg P3 (control of objectionable discharge), read with SANS 10400-P — water seals, traps and ventilation of the drainage installation are the deemed-to-satisfy means of keeping foul air out of the building 2. eThekwini Municipality Sewage Disposal By-law, 2016 s6 — discharge of offensive or odorous matter into the sewage disposal system prohibited 3. OHS Act 85 of 1993, Facilities Regulations 2004 reg 2 (sanitation) and reg 9 (condition of rooms and facilities: clean, hygienic, safe, whole and leak-free and in a good state of repair) — the duty the ablution cleaning and servicing records evidence 4. National Building Regulations reg A15(1)(a) — the owner must maintain any facility or service installation in the building in a safe and functional condition
evidenceExpected: Servicing/pump-out records for odour-generating components — grease traps, vent stacks, sump pump-outs — showing scheduled versus actual servicing dates.
target: No standalone SA regulation titled "odour control records" exists; this is the evidentiary counterpart of the objectionable-discharge requirement (SANS 10400-P Regulation P3) and applicable municipal wastewater by-laws. Odour management is practically evidenced through maintenance/service records of odour-generating components rather than a dedicated statutory record requirement.
walkabout: Check grease traps, vent stacks and sump pump-out points for odour and signs of overdue servicing (buildup, overflow staining), and compare against the servicing log dates.

requirement: Records for inspection of "Industrial Effluent" installations
basis: e.g Meters, Filtration Sumps, holding sumps
evidenceExpected: Trade-effluent discharge consent/permit from the local water services authority; meter-reading logs; sump inspection/desludging records; periodic effluent sample test results, checked against the permit's discharge limits.

A site of this kind also needs a trade-effluent discharge consent/permit from the local water services authority setting discharge quality limits (National Water Act ss21 & 39; municipal Wastewater/Industrial Effluent By-law).

acsaRequirement: T050 005M cl. 4.3 requires the AEMR to record all final effluent discharge points in the Register of Effluent and Storm Water Discharge Points EMS 105 and to implement an effluent quality analysis monitoring schedule. T050 006M requires all run-off from washing areas to be contained or channelled to an oil separator with a maintenance schedule implemented, servicing/refuelling areas to be bunded or sloped with a grease trap or oil separator before discharge to the sewer, and grease traps/separators to be monitored and cleaned. D060 012M cl. 4.5 sets the only numeric separator criteria in the whole set.
acsaThreshold: 'OIL SEPARATORS SHALL BE TESTED ANNUALLY FOR EFFICIENCY'; 'SLUDGE DEPTH SHALL NOT EXCEED 25% OF CHAMBER DEPTH'; 'DISPOSAL RECORDS SHALL BE RETAINED FOR 5 YEARS'; 'SPILL RESPONSE TIME SHALL NOT EXCEED 2 HOURS FOR CONTAINMENT' (D060 012M cl. 4.5 (a)-(d)). T050 006M states only that oil separators and grease traps be cleaned 'regularly' and that a maintenance schedule be implemented - no interval.
acsaEvidence: Register of Effluent and Storm Water Discharge Points - EMS 105
Effluent quality analysis monitoring schedule and results
Oil separator maintenance schedule and cleaning records
Annual oil separator efficiency test results
Hazardous waste manifests and Safe Disposal Certificates for separator sludge (retained 5 years)
acsaConflict: T050 006M mandates an oil-separator maintenance schedule and 'regular' grease trap cleaning but states no interval, and T050 005M requires an effluent monitoring schedule with no interval. Only D060 012M (a stormwater procedure) carries the annual efficiency test and the 25% sludge limit, so the auditor must import a stormwater clause to obtain a testable figure for industrial effluent installations. T050 004M and T050 006M also omit NEMA and the National Water Act from their legislation lists despite governing water pollution.

requirement: Records of installation tests ( PP26 or PP27)
basis: 1. National Building Regulations reg P7 (inspection and testing of drainage installations), read with SANS 10400-P — the installation must be inspected and tested before it is covered or used 2. SANS 10400-P cl. 4.26 (test for drains) — a drain shall be tested for watertightness by air test or water test in accordance with SANS 1200 LD 3. SANS 10400-P cl. 4.27 (test for discharge pipes and ventilating pipes) — tested for watertightness by air test or water test in accordance with SANS 10252-2 4. Water Services Act 108 of 1997 s21 and the eThekwini water services and sewage disposal by-laws — local-authority inspection and approval of the drainage installation before connection and covering
evidenceExpected: 1. Test certificate/record showing the drain test (PP26/clause 4.26) result, dated and signed off before the pipework was covered. 2. Test certificate/record showing the discharge/ventilating pipe test (PP27/clause 4.27) result, dated and signed off before the pipework was covered.
target: Two mandatory drainage installation tests under SANS 10400-P Regulation P7, both required before pipework is covered. 1. Drain Test (PP26/clause 4.26): drains must be air- or water-tested before being covered or used, with results verified and recorded. 2. Discharge & Ventilating Pipe Test (PP27/clause 4.27): discharge and ventilating pipes must be air- or water-tested before being covered or used, with results verified and recorded.
acsaConflict: No ACSA document requires drainage installation test certificates (municipal PP26 / PP27 forms or any equivalent hydraulic, air or water test on a completed drainage installation). D080 019M cl. 4.10 expressly states that calibration certificates are 'None required', and neither D080 019M nor D080 028M lists any commissioning or acceptance test for drainage. SANS 10252-2 is cited in the standards list of D080 019M but no clause of any ACSA procedure imports its testing requirements as an ACSA obligation.
basisNote: 'PP26' and 'PP27' are not SANS or National Building Regulations designations — the two tests are SANS 10400-P cl. 4.26 and 4.27, and the SANS 1200 LD test method they invoke survives in SANS 10400-P even though the wider SANS 1200 series has largely been replaced by SANS 2001 for new works.

requirement: Records of Maintenace Inspections & Job cards
basis: 1. National Building Regulations reg A15(1)(a) — the owner of a building must ensure that any mechanical equipment, facility or service installation provided in or in connection with the building is maintained in a safe and functional condition 2. OHS Act 85 of 1993, Construction Regulations 2014 reg 11(2)(c) and (d) — the structure and its installations must be kept safe for continued use, and records of inspections and maintenance kept and made available on request 3. OHS Act 85 of 1993 s8(1) and s8(2)(a) — provision and maintenance of a safe working environment and of systems of work and plant that are safe and without risks to health; the job card is the record of that maintenance 4. OHS Act, Facilities Regulations 2004 reg 9 — all rooms and facilities kept clean, hygienic, safe, whole and leak-free and in a good state of repair
evidenceExpected: CMMS job-card history for the asset for the last 12 months, showing scheduled versus completed maintenance inspections; ACSA's internal maintenance procedure defining required frequency/format.
target: No SA building regulation prescribes a specific job-card format or maintenance-record content. Legal basis is the OHS Act's general duty of care (s8) and Facilities Regulations 2004 reg 2(1) (facilities kept safe and in good repair). Maintenance inspection records and job cards are the practical evidence of this duty; format, frequency and retention are set by ACSA's own internal CMMS procedure.
walkabout: Select a sample of recently "completed" job cards and check on site whether the described work is actually evident (repaired item, replaced part); check whether any open job cards for visible defects remain unresolved.

Priority 2 High = failure will reduce or stop flight landings within eight (8) hours; Priority 3 Medium = services reduced within 24 hours (D060 016M cl. 4.1). Work orders, ME 038-041 and NOTAMs retained five (5) years (D060 016M cl. 11).

D060 016M has a Next Revision Date of 31 August 2026, which falls immediately before the audit window.
basisNote: The register's target text cites 'Facilities Regulations 2004 reg 2(1)' for the good-repair duty; reg 2 is sanitation — the maintenance duty is reg 9, 'Condition of rooms and facilities'.

acsaThreshold: 'ensuring checks are completed after EVERY rainfall event' in the rainy season (D060 012M cl. 4.1.6). Ponding risk response: SAME OPERATIONAL DAY; blocked inlet on runway/taxiway: IMMEDIATE (WITHIN 2 HOURS) (D060 012M cl. 4.5).

Annual trend analysis of repeat blockage zones and sediment sources
acsaConflict: The rainy-season rule is written as 'SHOULD increase the frequency' - permissive, not mandatory - and no pre-season deadline is set, so ACSA has no fixed date by which stormwater infrastructure must be cleared before the KwaZulu-Natal rainy season. The 'after every rainfall event' obligation is, however, absolute and directly testable.

requirement: Clearing & Maintenance programme
basis: e.g especially after rainfall events

Evidenced via ACSA's internal maintenance schedule/records, not a named external standard.
walkabout: Check the condition of stormwater infrastructure for evidence of recent clearing (versus accumulated silt/debris), and compare against the programme's stated schedule and the dates of recent significant rainfall events.

Contractor Compliance and Quality Assurance Audit - M&E 031 (monthly)
acsaConflict: D060 012M cl. 11 sets retention of the M&E 031 contractor audit at THREE (3) years in this procedure while every sibling D060 procedure sets FIVE (5) years for the same form - an internal retention inconsistency worth raising.

requirement: Check availability & effectiveness of Access points
basis: e.g Stormwater man-holes

walkabout: Locate each manhole/access chamber against the as-built drawings and check it is not paved/tarred over, is not silted up, and can be opened for inspection.

acsaRequirement: D060 012M cl. 4.1.4 requires the entire length of the catch pits to be inspected and, if required, cleaned, with inlets or entrance grids cleared of all debris and vegetation and a check that 'inlets are secure, safe and grids are in place'. Where weed killer introduces soil erosion issues it must be discontinued for a period to allow vegetation cover to grow and provide protection. Blocked access points on the movement area attract the cl. 4.5 defect response times.
acsaThreshold: Catch pit inspection and cleaning: Six Monthly (6M) (cl. 4.1.4). Weed killer to a minimum two (2) metre radius around catch pits (cl. 4.1.4). 'BLOCKED INLET ON RUNWAY/TAXIWAY - IMMEDIATE (WITHIN 2 HOURS)' (cl. 4.5).

Defect records and response times for blocked inlets
Oracle eAM work orders raised against blocked or missing grids
acsaConflict: ACSA sets no requirement for access-chamber spacing, manhole cover load rating, or a register of stormwater access points, and no confined-space entry requirement is written into D060 012M for entry into stormwater chambers (S010 007M Confined Spaces Entry is cross-referenced in the related-documents list but is not part of the 99-document set).

requirement: Maintenance of Water Infrastructure & Quality of water
basis: SANS 241
evidenceExpected: 1. Most recent drinking-water quality test certificate(s) against SANS 241 limits; where ACSA operates its own borehole/reticulation, the sampling schedule/procedure. 2. Proof non-potable outlets are clearly marked.
target: Two water-quality requirements. 1. Drinking Water Quality: SANS 241 sets maximum allowable and aesthetic limits for microbiological, physical, aesthetic and chemical determinands; Facilities Regulations 2004 require an employer to supply water meeting this standard. Where municipally supplied, the municipality is primarily responsible; where ACSA operates its own boreholes/reticulation, ACSA is responsible for periodic (risk-based, commonly quarterly-to-annual) sampling against SANS 241 limits — confirm exact frequency against ACSA's own procedure. 2. Non-Potable Outlet Marking: any non-potable pipework/taps (irrigation, industrial use) must be clearly marked as such.
question: 1. Is this site's water supply municipal or ACSA-operated (borehole/reticulation) — and if ACSA-operated, is SANS 241 sampling actually being carried out against a defined schedule?
walkabout: 2. Walk the site identifying any non-potable outlets (irrigation taps, industrial-use points) and check each carries clear, legible marking distinguishing it from potable water.

acsaRequirement: D080 014M requires water quality sampling and testing on the water tank asset group, and singles out King Shaka: sampling and testing is MONTHLY at FALE where the rest of the network is tri-monthly. Aircraft watering points must be inspected DAILY per the approved contractor's task list (outage required) as well as three-monthly. The water reticulation system is inspected monthly (main line and internal valves for wear and damage, water meters for proper operation, power to control alive, chemical feed tube condition and chemical sufficiency) and water tanks tri-monthly for leaks, corrosion, pump operation, valve function and filter cleaning. At FALE the applicable asset groups are TKW, WTT, WPA and WRS; WTS (Water Treatment) is N/A.
acsaThreshold: 'Sample water and test the water quality' - 'FALE Only - Done Monthly' against Tri-Monthly (3M) elsewhere (D080 014M cl. 4.6.1 item 7). Watering Point - Aircraft (WPA): inspection Daily (D) plus Tri-Monthly (3M) (cl. 4.5 / 4.6.3). System - Water Reticulation (WRS): Monthly (M) (cl. 4.5 / 4.6.4). Tank - Water (TKW) and Tower/Reservoir (WTT): Tri-Monthly (3M) (cl. 4.5 / 4.6.1, 4.6.2).
acsaEvidence: Monthly water quality sampling and test results for FALE (cl. 4.6.1 item 7)
Daily aircraft watering point inspection sheets (approved contractor task list)
Monthly water reticulation inspection records including water meter operation
Tri-monthly water tank and reservoir inspection records
Contractor Compliance and Quality Assurance Audit - ME 031 (monthly)
Approved contractor task lists / inspection sheets for WTT and WPA
acsaConflict: D080 014M mandates water quality testing but cites NO potable-water quality standard at all - SANS 241 is entirely absent from its referenced standards, which list only SANS 10252-2:1993, SANS 10254:2004 and SANS 10400:1990 (the last two superseded editions). ACSA therefore requires monthly sampling at KSIA against no stated pass/fail criteria, and cl. 4.10 'b) Calibration Certificates' appears as a blank heading with no content. The records table also misnumbers the procedure as 'D080 009M', and cl. 4.4 refers to 'preventative maintenance on Sewer Systems' - copy-paste from D080 019M.

siteVariant.note: 'Sample water and test the water quality' - 'FALE Only - Done Monthly' against Tri-Monthly (3M) elsewhere (D080 014M cl. 4.6.1 item 7). Watering Point - Aircraft (WPA): inspection Daily (D) plus Tri-Monthly (3M) (cl. 4.5 / 4.6.3). System - Water Reticulation (WRS): Monthly (M) (cl. 4.5 / 4.6.4). Tank - Water (TKW) and Tower/Reservoir (WTT): Tri-Monthly (3M) (cl. 4.5 / 4.6.1, 4.6.2).

requirement: Hot-water temperatures, odour control, backflow prevention, leak detection, ablution fixtures functional.
basis: SANS 10252-1; SANS 10254; SANS 893
evidenceExpected: Inspection; maintenance records
target: Compliant
question: 1. What outlet temperature do hot water systems in ablution/kitchen areas actually deliver, and does ACSA have a defined safe-temperature target they are being checked against?
walkabout: 1. Check a sample of hot water outlets with a thermometer (or ask staff to demonstrate a recent reading). 2. Walk ablution areas and note any persistent drain/sewer odour. 3. Locate backflow prevention devices at key connection points and check for a current test tag/label. 4. Test a sample of ablution fixtures for correct operation and check for visible leaks, drips or damage.
